rewrites.blindSummary:
No regional protective statute, recorded incident series or documented enforcement divergence from the national framework has been documented for this state/province. The national framework applies in full: a 2014 statute punishes same-sex unions with up to 14 years' imprisonment and — as reported in August 2026 summarising a foreign government's travel advisory — also reaches assisting, attending or promoting same-sex ceremonies and LGBT+ organisations; religious criminal law in some state/provinces can carry the death penalty for same-sex conduct. The same advisory warns LGBT+ travellers to this country of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation.

The recorded violence pattern is national and recent: a 33-year-old transgender media personality and sex worker was beaten to death in the national capital in August 2024, having reported a stabbing a year earlier and said she feared for her life; authorities ordered a discreet investigation. Mass arrests and detention of LGBT+ people remain common, concentrated in some state/provinces. The framework also bans public expression of identity and LGBT+ organising, and the advisory additionally flags short-notice curfews, network shutdowns and communal violence. The absence of state/province-specific records here reflects thin documentation rather than demonstrated safety.
rewrites.blindTangential: The 2014 same-sex marriage prohibition law (up to 14 years, applies to tourists, bans LGBTQ+ organisations and public expression) shapes police and prosecutorial posture toward anyone perceived as same-sex-active, including gender-nonconforming visitors, everywhere in this country including this division; dating-app extortion gangs present a documented app-user risk to gay and trans people alike. The separate religious-law death-penalty regime for same-sex conduct applies only in some state/provinces, not in this division.
rewrites.blindOutOfScope: Armed insurgency, kidnapping and violent crime affect travellers in many parts of the country; these are general hazards, not trans-specific.

An allied government's August 2026 travel advice warns LGBT+ travellers nationwide of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation.

Trans-specific risk is documented nationally: a national broadcaster reported mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people as common, especially in some state/provinces, and the killing of a prominent transgender creator in the capital in August 2024 — found beaten beside a highway hours after saying she was going out, a year after a stabbing she had said left her fearing for her life — evidences lethal violence against visibly trans people, with a promised investigation but no accountability recorded in the sources.

No state/province-specific sources for this division survived audit, so no local divergence is claimed; sources do not name this division among the religious-criminal-law state/provinces, but it sits nearest to where those provisions operate, and the national penalties apply throughout.
rewrites.blindTangential: This state/province sits between the country's two criminal-law systems: its neighbouring state/provinces include members of the criminal-law block, so a visitor crossing into them changes criminal-law system, arresting authority (police plus religious police) and penalties (the national law's 14 years versus lashes or stoning), while this state/province's own law remains the uniform national law.
blindSourceSummaries: A news report (9 Aug 2024) on the death of a 33-year-old transgender creator in this country: her beaten body was found along a highway in the capital, suspected murder, roughly a year after she had said she feared for her life; an investigation was announced. The article notes that despite formal constitutional guarantees of non-discrimination and private/family life, mass arrests and detention of LGBTQ+ people are common, especially in some state/provinces — national-climate evidence the record's summary relies on for this state/province.

A foreign government's travel advisory (19 Aug 2026) warns LGBT+ travellers to this country of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, stating that same-sex sexual activity is illegal and can attract up to 14 years' imprisonment, and that the national law extends to people who arrange, attend or conduct same-sex weddings and those involved with gay groups or organisations. It adds that some state/provinces operate religious criminal law under which same-sex activity can attract the death penalty, and that breaching curfews or movement restrictions risks arrest and detention. National-framework facts the record's own summary claims for this state/province.

blindSourceSummaries: A foreign government's country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity for this country (June 2025) is the national framework this division is scored against: consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned; the national supreme court designated the international LGBT+ movement an 'extremist' organisation in November 2023; between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement, with 'gay propaganda' fines or 15 days' detention for individuals, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023. The note contains no division-specific information beyond that national framework.

A rights organisation (30 June 2025): the country's courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions for participation in the international LGBT movement or displaying its symbols since the national supreme court's November 2023 designation, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison; the organisation also documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media. This national enforcement baseline underpins the national score this division is assessed at; the article contains no division-specific detail.

Nationally: same-sex marriage and gender transition banned, the November 2023 'extremist' designation of the LGBT+ movement, at least 139 individuals affected by enforcement in 2022-2024. The note does not cover the murder case in this record's summary.

A rights organisation (30 June 2025): nationally, the country's courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions connected to the international LGBT movement since its November 2023 designation (defendants face up to 12 years in prison), and 81 people in 98 cases have been found guilty since January 2024 of administrative offences for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media. The article's only mention of this city is a photo caption of a local Pride rally of 3 August 2019; it does not cover the murder case in this record's summary.

An encyclopaedia biography documents the city-level origin of the anti-LGBT law a trans visitor to this city stands under: as a member of the city's legislative assembly (2007-2016) the subject is recorded as the principal sponsor of the legislation criminalising 'homosexual propaganda directed toward minors' - the city ban enacted in 2012 that a cited news report (29 February 2012) covered, with the page quoting the subject's statement that he fully intended to catch a visiting pop performer committing a possible offence under it. The page also records the subject stating in 2013 that gay athletes could be arrested at an international sporting event the following year if they promoted homosexuality to minors, and his protests against the city's local LGBT film festival in November 2013. This is the most jurisdiction-specific enforcement origin available for the record's local assessment of LGBT-hostile measures in the city.

An encyclopaedia's country overview supplies the national framework this city is assessed under: a 2013 law criminalises distributing 'propaganda' of 'non-traditional sexual relationships' among minors, with organisations facing up to 90 days' suspension and foreigners up to 15 days' detention and deportation. The page records that ten regions including this city (2012) enacted regional versions of the ban before the national law, and that this city removed its regional law in 2014, leaving the national statute in force there. It also notes a July 2023 law banning gender transition outright - prohibiting both gender-affirming surgery and legal gender recognition - and a 2010 ruling by a regional human-rights court fining the country over the systematic refusal of pride-event permits. This grounds the record's national-score anchor with dated, sourced specifics.
